directAnswer: Pope Damasus II was Poppo, a Bavarian-born bishop of Brixen whom Emperor Henry III nominated to the papacy. He was consecrated on July 17, 1048, and died on August 9, 1048, after a reign of only about three weeks, one of the shortest in the Church's history.

sections.h2: Poppo of Brixen and the Emperor's Choice
paras: Before his election, Poppo served as bishop of Brixen (today Bressanone in South Tyrol), a see closely tied to the German imperial court. In the 1040s the papacy had been fought over by Roman noble factions, and Benedict IX had returned to Rome yet again after the death of Clement II in 1047.

Henry III, who had already intervened at the Synod of Sutri in 1046, named Poppo as the next pope and had Benedict removed. Poppo was installed in Rome and took the name Damasus II, recalling the fourth-century Pope St. Damasus I. He was the second of the German bishops placed on the papal throne through Henry's influence.

sections.h2: Twenty-Three Days and a Death at Palestrina
paras: Damasus left almost no record as pope. Within weeks of his consecration he withdrew from the summer heat of Rome to Palestrina, where he died on August 9, 1048. Historians usually suspect malaria, which was common in the region in summer. Rumors of poisoning circulated at the time, but no reliable evidence supports them.

His brief reign matters mainly for what came next. After his death the emperor turned to his kinsman Bruno of Toul, who became Leo IX and launched the reform movement that reshaped the eleventh-century Church. Beyond his appointment and his death, the sources tell us very little about Damasus II himself.

keyFacts: Personal name: Poppo, bishop of Brixen
Born in Bavaria, at Pildenau according to tradition
Consecrated July 17, 1048; died August 9, 1048, at Palestrina
Nominated by Emperor Henry III after the removal of Benedict IX
Succeeded by Leo IX, who began the Gregorian reform era

faqs.question: Why was Pope Damasus II's reign so short?
faqs.answer: He died at Palestrina roughly three weeks after his consecration. The cause is not recorded with certainty; malaria is the most common explanation, while contemporary rumors of poison remain unproven.

faqs.question: Who chose Damasus II as pope?
faqs.answer: Emperor Henry III of Germany nominated him, as part of the emperor's effort to end the disputes over the papacy among Roman noble families and the repeated returns of Benedict IX.

directAnswer: Pope St. Leo IX was Bruno of Egisheim-Dagsburg, an Alsatian nobleman and bishop of Toul who reigned from 1049 to 1054. He made the papacy the driving force of Church reform against simony and clerical marriage, traveled widely holding synods, and died just weeks before his legates and the Patriarch of Constantinople exchanged the excommunications of 1054.

sections.h2: From Bishop of Toul to Pilgrim Pope
paras: Bruno was born in 1002 into the family of the counts of Egisheim in Alsace and was related to the imperial house. He became bishop of Toul in 1026 and governed that diocese for more than twenty years, gaining a reputation for pastoral care and for supporting monastic reform.

When Emperor Henry III proposed him for the papacy at Worms in late 1048, Bruno accepted only on condition that the clergy and people of Rome freely confirm the choice. He traveled to Rome dressed as a pilgrim and was enthroned in February 1049. That gesture signaled that a pope's authority should rest on canonical election, not imperial appointment alone.

sections.h2: A Traveling Reformer and His Circle
paras: Leo IX spent much of his pontificate on the road. He held synods in Rome, at Reims and at Mainz in 1049 and in many other cities, where bishops and abbots were examined for simony, the buying and selling of Church offices. Clerical marriage and concubinage were also condemned. At Rome and Vercelli in 1050, synods rejected the eucharistic teaching of Berengar of Tours.

He gathered able reformers around him, including Humbert of Silva Candida, Frederick of Lorraine, and a young Roman cleric named Hildebrand, the future Gregory VII. Through them the College of Cardinals began to take on an international character and a central role in governing the Church.

sections.h2: Civitate and Captivity Among the Normans
paras: Norman adventurers were seizing land in southern Italy, and Leo tried to stop them by force. In June 1053 his army was defeated at the Battle of Civitate, and the pope was held by the Normans at Benevento for about nine months. Many contemporaries criticized a pope leading troops, and Leo himself is said to have grieved over the dead.
Released in March 1054 and in poor health, he returned to Rome and died there on April 19, 1054.

sections.h2: The Legation to Constantinople and 1054
paras: Before his death Leo sent Cardinal Humbert to Constantinople to address disputes with Patriarch Michael Cerularius over azymes (unleavened bread), customs and Roman primacy. On July 16, 1054, Humbert laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the patriarch answered with anathemas of his own. Because Leo had already died, historians debate whether the legates still had authority to act.

These events became the symbolic date of the East-West Schism, though the separation developed over a longer period. On December 7, 1965, Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I issued a joint declaration removing the mutual excommunications from the Church's memory. Leo IX is venerated as a saint, with a feast day on April 19.

keyFacts: Born Bruno of Egisheim-Dagsburg in Alsace in 1002; bishop of Toul from 1026
Reigned February 12, 1049 – April 19, 1054
Held reform synods at Rome, Reims, Mainz and elsewhere against simony
Defeated by the Normans at Civitate in 1053 and held captive at Benevento
His legate Humbert's excommunication of Michael Cerularius (1054) marks the East-West Schism
Venerated as a saint; feast day April 19

faqs.question: Did Pope Leo IX cause the East-West Schism?
faqs.answer: Not directly. He sent the legation to Constantinople, but the bull of excommunication was placed on the altar of Hagia Sophia in July 1054, about three months after his death. The schism also grew out of centuries of theological, cultural and political tension.

faqs.question: Why is Leo IX considered a reforming pope?
faqs.answer: He used councils across Europe to fight simony and clerical marriage, insisted on canonical election to the papacy, and brought reformers such as Humbert and Hildebrand into the Roman Church, laying the groundwork for the Gregorian reform.

faqs.question: Why was Pope Leo IX captured by the Normans?
faqs.answer: He led an army against Norman forces in southern Italy and was defeated at Civitate in June 1053. The Normans held him at Benevento with outward respect until March 1054.

directAnswer: Pope Victor II was Gebhard, bishop of Eichstätt and a trusted adviser to Emperor Henry III, who reigned from 1055 to 1057. He continued Leo IX's campaign against simony and, after the emperor's death in 1056, helped secure the succession of the boy king Henry IV.

sections.h2: Gebhard of Eichstätt, the Emperor's Counselor
paras: Gebhard came from a Swabian-Bavarian noble family and was made bishop of Eichstätt while still young. He became one of Henry III's closest political advisers, which made him an unlikely candidate for Rome: the emperor was reluctant to lose him. After the death of Leo IX, Roman envoys led by Hildebrand pressed for Gebhard, and he was consecrated on April 13, 1055, taking the name Victor II.
He was the last of the four German popes whose elevation depended on Henry III.

sections.h2: The Synod of Florence and Henry III's Deathbed
paras: In 1055 Victor and the emperor presided together at a synod in Florence that renewed the condemnations of simony and clerical marriage and addressed the alienation of Church property. Victor kept Leo IX's reforming team in place and sent legates to France on the same program.

In 1056 he traveled to Germany and was present when Henry III died in October of that year. Victor helped the widowed Empress Agnes secure the throne for six-year-old Henry IV and worked to reconcile German princes. Returning to Italy, he died at Arezzo on July 28, 1057. The surviving record covers mainly these political services; little is known of his personal piety or writings.

keyFacts: Personal name: Gebhard, bishop of Eichstätt
Reigned April 13, 1055 – July 28, 1057
Presided with Henry III at the reform Synod of Florence (1055)
Attended Henry III's death in 1056 and supported the regency for Henry IV
Died at Arezzo

faqs.question: What was Victor II's role after Emperor Henry III died?
faqs.answer: He was at the emperor's side in 1056 and helped Empress Agnes secure the succession of the young Henry IV, acting as a stabilizing figure among the German princes.

faqs.question: Did Victor II continue Leo IX's reforms?
faqs.answer: Yes. He kept Leo's advisers, presided at the Synod of Florence against simony and clerical marriage, and sent legates to enforce reform decrees.

directAnswer: Pope Stephen IX was Frederick of Lorraine, a reforming cardinal and abbot of Monte Cassino who reigned from August 1057 to March 1058. He was elected in Rome without waiting for imperial approval, strengthened the reform party, and was the last German-born pope until Benedict XVI.

sections.h2: Frederick of Lorraine and Monte Cassino
paras: Frederick was a younger brother of Godfrey the Bearded, duke of Lorraine and one of the most powerful men in Italy. Under Leo IX he served as chancellor of the Roman Church and joined Cardinal Humbert on the 1054 legation to Constantinople. Afterward he became a monk at Monte Cassino and was elected its abbot in 1057, shortly before Victor II made him cardinal priest of San Crisogono.

When news of Victor's death reached Rome, the clergy and people chose Frederick on August 2, 1057, without first consulting the German court, a sign of the reformers' growing independence. He kept the abbacy of Monte Cassino as pope.

sections.h2: A Brief Reform Pontificate
paras: During his eight months Stephen promoted leading reformers, most notably naming Peter Damian cardinal bishop of Ostia. He continued the campaign against simony and clerical marriage. Some sources report that he considered steps to strengthen his brother's position in Italy, but such plans remain uncertain.

He fell ill and died at Florence on March 29, 1058. His death opened the way for the Tusculan faction to install the antipope Benedict X. His numbering varies: because a pope-elect named Stephen died in 752 before consecration, some lists call him Stephen X.

keyFacts: Personal name: Frederick of Lorraine, brother of Duke Godfrey the Bearded
Reigned August 2, 1057 – March 29, 1058
Abbot of Monte Cassino; a Benedictine monk
Member of the 1054 legation to Constantinople
Named Peter Damian cardinal bishop of Ostia
Last German pope before Benedict XVI; sometimes numbered Stephen X

faqs.question: Why is Stephen IX sometimes called Stephen X?
faqs.answer: A man elected pope as Stephen in 752 died before his consecration. Lists that count him number later Stephens one higher, so Frederick of Lorraine appears as either Stephen IX or Stephen X.

faqs.question: Was Stephen IX elected with the emperor's approval?
faqs.answer: No. The Roman clergy and people elected him immediately after Victor II's death without consulting the German court, which the reform party saw as an assertion of the Church's freedom.

directAnswer: Pope Nicholas II was Gerard of Burgundy, bishop of Florence, who reigned from 1058 to 1061. He is best remembered for the 1059 decree In nomine Domini, which placed papal elections chiefly in the hands of the cardinals, and for allying the papacy with the Normans of southern Italy.

sections.h2: Gerard of Florence and the Contest With Benedict X
paras: Gerard was a Burgundian cleric, born in the region of Savoy, who became bishop of Florence around 1045. After the death of Stephen IX in 1058, Roman nobles of the Tusculan family installed John Mincius, bishop of Velletri, as Benedict X. The reform cardinals, guided by Hildebrand and with the support of Godfrey of Lorraine, met at Siena and elected Gerard in December 1058.
With military backing, Nicholas entered Rome early in 1059, and Benedict X was driven out and later deposed. The episode convinced the reformers that the method of electing popes had to be changed.

sections.h2: In nomine Domini and the Cardinals' Role
paras: At a Lateran synod in April 1059, Nicholas issued the decree In nomine Domini. It gave the cardinal bishops the leading role in choosing a pope, after which the other cardinals would join them and the clergy and people of Rome would give their assent. The decree allowed the election to take place outside Rome if conditions there prevented a free vote, and it mentioned the honor due to the German king in vague terms.
Though modified over time, the decree is the foundation of the system in which the College of Cardinals elects the pope, a system that continues today in the conclave.

sections.h2: The Treaty of Melfi and the Norman Alliance
paras: Nicholas reversed Leo IX's hostility toward the Normans. At Melfi in August 1059 he invested Robert Guiscard as duke of Apulia and Calabria, and of Sicily once he conquered it, and recognized Richard of Aversa as prince of Capua. In return the Normans swore fealty to the pope and promised to protect papal elections. This alliance gave the reform papacy military protection independent of the emperor.
The same synod of 1059 required Berengar of Tours to affirm a strongly worded profession of faith on the Real Presence in the Eucharist, and it renewed decrees against simony and clerical marriage.

sections.h2: Death at Florence and an Imperial Backlash
paras: Nicholas kept his see of Florence while pope and died there on July 27, 1061. His policies, especially the election decree, alarmed the German court, which had not been consulted. That tension surfaced immediately in the disputed election that followed his death, when an imperial party set up a rival claimant against Alexander II.

keyFacts: Personal name: Gerard of Burgundy, bishop of Florence
Reigned December 6, 1058 – July 27, 1061
Elected at Siena in opposition to the antipope Benedict X
Issued In nomine Domini (1059), the decree giving cardinals the chief role in papal elections
Treaty of Melfi (1059) made the Norman leaders papal vassals
Died at Florence

faqs.question: What did the decree In nomine Domini do?
faqs.answer: Issued in 1059, it made the cardinal bishops the principal electors of the pope, followed by the other cardinals, with the Roman clergy and people assenting. It is the origin of election by the College of Cardinals.

faqs.question: Why did Nicholas II ally with the Normans?
faqs.answer: The reform papacy needed protection from Roman nobles and independence from the German court. By investing Norman leaders with lands in southern Italy at Melfi in 1059, he gained vassals sworn to defend the Holy See.

faqs.question: Who was Benedict X?
faqs.answer: He was John Mincius, installed by Roman nobles in 1058. The reform cardinals considered his election uncanonical, and he is counted as an antipope.

directAnswer: Pope Alexander II was Anselm of Baggio, a Milanese reformer and bishop of Lucca who reigned from 1061 to 1073. The first pope chosen under the cardinals' election decree of 1059, he overcame the imperial antipope Honorius II, advanced the reform program, and supported William of Normandy's claim to England.

sections.h2: Anselm of Baggio and the Milanese Pataria
paras: Anselm came from a noble family near Milan. As a cleric there he sympathized with the Pataria, a popular movement that opposed simony and married clergy in the Milanese church. He became bishop of Lucca in 1057 and served on papal missions to Milan alongside Peter Damian.
He kept the bishopric of Lucca throughout his pontificate, and his experience of Milan's conflicts shaped his support for reform movements that challenged entrenched local clergy.

sections.h2: The Election of 1061 and the Antipope Cadalus
paras: After Nicholas II died, the cardinals, with Hildebrand's backing, elected Anselm on September 30, 1061, following the new decree and without waiting for the German court. In response, the regency for the young Henry IV and a group of Lombard bishops chose Cadalus, bishop of Parma, who took the name Honorius II.

Cadalus's supporters fought their way into Rome more than once, and the schism lasted several years. A council at Mantua in 1064 recognized Alexander as the rightful pope, and support for Cadalus faded.

sections.h2: England, Spain and the Reach of Papal Authority
paras: Alexander gave his blessing to William of Normandy's invasion of England in 1066; chroniclers report that William fought under a papal banner. In 1070 papal legates crowned William again at Easter and presided over councils that removed Archbishop Stigand of Canterbury, opening the way for Lanfranc. Historians continue to debate how far papal support reflected reform goals and how far it served Norman ambitions.

In Spain, Alexander wrote to bishops commending them for protecting Jews from violence during campaigns against Muslim rulers, distinguishing between peaceful Jewish communities and those at war with Christians. That letter became an important reference in later canon law. He also extended papal oversight across Europe through legates, a practice his successor would expand.

sections.h2: Hildebrand's Partnership and Alexander's Death
paras: Throughout the reign Hildebrand served as archdeacon and principal adviser, and many contemporaries saw him as the strongest figure in the Curia. Alexander nonetheless acted as an independent pastor and judge, ruling on marriage cases and disciplinary disputes across Christendom.
Alexander died in Rome on April 21, 1073. During his funeral the next day, crowds acclaimed Hildebrand as his successor, who became Gregory VII.

keyFacts: Personal name: Anselm of Baggio, bishop of Lucca
Reigned September 30, 1061 – April 21, 1073
First pope elected under the 1059 decree In nomine Domini
Opposed by the antipope Honorius II (Cadalus of Parma); upheld by the Council of Mantua (1064)
Supported William of Normandy's invasion of England (1066)
Succeeded by his archdeacon Hildebrand, Gregory VII

faqs.question: Did Pope Alexander II approve the Norman Conquest?
faqs.answer: He backed William of Normandy's claim to the English throne, and chroniclers say William carried a papal banner in 1066. Papal legates later took part in reorganizing the English Church under William.

faqs.question: Who was the antipope during Alexander II's reign?
faqs.answer: Cadalus, bishop of Parma, was elected by imperial supporters in 1061 as Honorius II. The Council of Mantua in 1064 decided in Alexander's favor.

faqs.question: What was Alexander II's connection to Milan?
faqs.answer: He was Milanese by birth and supported the Pataria, a reform movement there that opposed simony and married clergy.

directAnswer: Pope St. Gregory VII was Hildebrand of Sovana, the reform leader who reigned from 1073 to 1085. He fought simony, clerical marriage and lay investiture, clashed with Emperor Henry IV in the Investiture Controversy, received the emperor's penance at Canossa in 1077, and died in exile at Salerno.

sections.h2: Hildebrand, Architect of Reform
paras: Hildebrand was born in Tuscany, at Sovana, probably between 1015 and 1020, and was educated in Rome. He served Gregory VI and followed him into exile in Germany in 1047. Returning with Leo IX in 1049, he spent the next quarter century at the center of the reform papacy as subdeacon, legate and finally archdeacon, advising Leo IX, Victor II, Stephen IX, Nicholas II and Alexander II.

He is often described as a monk, though where and when he took vows is debated. On April 22, 1073, during the funeral of Alexander II, the Roman crowd acclaimed him pope, and the cardinals confirmed the choice. He took the name Gregory, likely in honor of Gregory VI and of St. Gregory the Great.

sections.h2: The Gregorian Reform and the Dictatus Papae
paras: Gregory pressed the reform program harder than any predecessor. Synods in Rome condemned simony and required clergy to live celibate lives, and the faithful were told not to attend Masses of priests living openly in violation of these rules. Legates carried the decrees across Europe, often meeting fierce resistance from clergy and nobles.

His register for 1075 contains the Dictatus Papae, a list of twenty-seven brief propositions on papal authority. Among them: that the Roman pontiff alone is rightly called universal, that he may depose emperors, and that the Roman Church has never erred. Scholars debate whether it was a policy statement or headings for a canon law collection, but it shows how Gregory understood the pope's place in Christendom.

sections.h2: Henry IV and the Road to Canossa
paras: The Lenten synod of 1075 condemned lay investiture, the practice of kings appointing bishops and investing them with ring and staff. When Henry IV continued naming bishops, including in Milan, Gregory rebuked him. In January 1076 a synod of German bishops at Worms declared Gregory deposed. Gregory answered at his Lenten synod by excommunicating Henry and releasing his subjects from their oaths of allegiance.

With German princes threatening to replace him, Henry crossed the Alps in winter and came to the castle of Countess Matilda of Tuscany at Canossa, where Gregory was staying. In January 1077 he waited outside as a penitent for three days, and Gregory, as a priest bound to absolve a repentant sinner, lifted the excommunication.

sections.h2: Second Excommunication, the Sack of Rome and Exile
paras: The reconciliation did not last. German princes elected Rudolf of Rheinfelden as rival king, and in 1080 Gregory excommunicated Henry again. Henry responded by having Archbishop Guibert of Ravenna elected as antipope Clement III. In 1084 Henry captured Rome and Guibert crowned him emperor, while Gregory held out in Castel Sant'Angelo.

Robert Guiscard's Normans rescued the pope, but their troops sacked parts of the city, turning Romans against him. Gregory withdrew to Salerno, where he died on May 25, 1085. Tradition attributes to him the dying words that he had loved justice and hated iniquity and therefore died in exile, an echo of Psalm 45.

sections.h2: Canonization and Lasting Influence
paras: Gregory VII is venerated as a saint, and his feast is kept on May 25. The struggle he began was settled only in 1122 by the Concordat of Worms, but his insistence on the freedom of the Church from lay control, on clerical discipline and on the authority of the Holy See shaped Western Christianity for centuries.

keyFacts: Born Hildebrand at Sovana in Tuscany, about 1015–1020
Reigned April 22, 1073 – May 25, 1085
Banned lay investiture (1075) and issued the Dictatus Papae
Excommunicated Henry IV in 1076 and absolved him at Canossa in January 1077
Opposed by the antipope Clement III (Guibert of Ravenna) from 1080
Died in exile at Salerno; venerated as a saint, feast May 25

faqs.question: What happened at Canossa in 1077?
faqs.answer: Excommunicated Emperor Henry IV came to Countess Matilda's castle at Canossa, where Gregory VII was staying, and stood as a penitent for three days in January 1077. Gregory then absolved him, though their conflict resumed a few years later.

faqs.question: What is the Dictatus Papae?
faqs.answer: It is a list of twenty-seven short statements on papal authority found in Gregory VII's register for 1075, including claims that the pope may depose emperors and that the Roman Church has never erred.

faqs.question: Why did Gregory VII die in exile?
faqs.answer: After Henry IV took Rome in 1084, Gregory's Norman allies rescued him but sacked parts of the city. Facing hostility from the Romans, he withdrew to Salerno, where he died in 1085.

directAnswer: Blessed Victor III was Desiderius, the celebrated abbot of Monte Cassino, who reigned as pope from 1086 to 1087. A reluctant pope who was consecrated only a year after his election, he condemned lay investiture at the Synod of Benevento and died at his abbey a few months later.

sections.h2: Desiderius and the Golden Age of Monte Cassino
paras: Born around 1027 into the Lombard princely family of Benevento, Daufer (as he was first called) fled an arranged marriage to pursue the monastic life and took the name Desiderius. He became abbot of Monte Cassino in 1058, succeeding Frederick of Lorraine, who had become Stephen IX.

Under Desiderius the abbey reached the height of its influence. He rebuilt its basilica, which Alexander II consecrated in 1071, bringing artisans from Constantinople for mosaics and bronze work. The library and scriptorium flourished, producing manuscripts in the distinctive Beneventan script. He also wrote Dialogues on the miracles of St. Benedict.

sections.h2: Mediator Between Popes and Normans
paras: Monte Cassino lay in Norman territory, and Desiderius became a key go-between linking the papacy to Robert Guiscard and Richard of Capua. Gregory VII made him a cardinal, and he helped reconcile the Normans with the reform popes, though his willingness to negotiate with Henry IV in the 1080s made some Gregorians distrust him.

sections.h2: A Reluctant Election
paras: After Gregory VII's death, the cardinals pressed Desiderius to accept the papacy. Elected on May 24, 1086, he soon laid aside the papal insignia and returned to his abbey, and for months refused to act as pope. Only in March 1087, at a synod at Capua, did he agree to take up the office. He was consecrated in Rome on May 9, 1087, while the antipope Clement III's partisans still held parts of the city.

sections.h2: The Synod of Benevento and Death at His Abbey
paras: In August 1087 Victor held a synod at Benevento that renewed the condemnation of lay investiture and excommunicated the antipope Clement III. That year he also supported an expedition of Pisan and Genoese fleets against Mahdia in North Africa, which sailed under a papal banner.

Falling ill at the synod, he returned to Monte Cassino and died there on September 16, 1087, having recommended Odo of Ostia, the future Urban II, as his successor. He was buried at the abbey, and his cult was confirmed by Pope Leo XIII in 1887.

keyFacts: Born at Benevento around 1027; abbot of Monte Cassino from 1058
Elected May 24, 1086; consecrated May 9, 1087; died September 16, 1087
Rebuilt the basilica of Monte Cassino, consecrated in 1071
Synod of Benevento (1087) condemned lay investiture and the antipope Clement III
Benedictine monk; beatified (cult confirmed) by Leo XIII in 1887

faqs.question: Why did Victor III delay taking office?
faqs.answer: He was reluctant to leave Monte Cassino and to take on the papacy amid the conflict with Henry IV and the antipope Clement III. He accepted only in March 1087, nearly a year after his election.

faqs.question: What is Victor III known for as abbot?
faqs.answer: As Abbot Desiderius he made Monte Cassino a major center of art and learning, rebuilding its basilica with Byzantine artisans and fostering a productive scriptorium.

faqs.question: Is Victor III a saint?
faqs.answer: He is a blessed. Pope Leo XIII confirmed his cult in 1887.

directAnswer: Blessed Urban II was Odo of Châtillon, a French monk of Cluny who reigned as pope from 1088 to 1099. He restored the reform papacy after the struggles of Gregory VII's last years and launched the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont in 1095, dying two weeks after crusaders captured Jerusalem.

sections.h2: From Reims and Cluny to Ostia
paras: Odo was born around 1035 in Champagne, near Châtillon-sur-Marne, to a knightly family. He studied at Reims, where St. Bruno, later founder of the Carthusians, was among the teachers, and he served as archdeacon there. He then entered the abbey of Cluny and became its prior under Abbot Hugh.
Gregory VII called him to Rome around 1080 and made him cardinal bishop of Ostia. He served as legate in Germany, where he worked to rally supporters of reform against Henry IV.

sections.h2: Rebuilding a Divided Papacy
paras: Rome was held by the antipope Clement III when Odo was elected at Terracina on March 12, 1088. For years Urban could live in Rome only intermittently. He combined firmness on the principles of reform with a flexible diplomacy, winning back bishops and princes who had wavered and gradually isolating the antipope.

His pontificate also saw the Roman Curia take a more organized form, and the term curia itself becomes common in papal documents in this period. Urban held numerous synods in Italy and France, and he excommunicated King Philip I of France over his marriage to Bertrade of Montfort.

sections.h2: Piacenza, Clermont and the First Crusade
paras: At the Council of Piacenza in March 1095, envoys of the Byzantine emperor Alexios I asked for Western help against the Seljuk Turks. In November 1095 Urban held a council at Clermont in France, and on November 27 he preached in an open field, calling knights to go to the aid of Eastern Christians and to free Jerusalem. Those who went for devotion rather than for glory or gain were promised that the journey would count in place of all penance.

No text of the sermon survives from that day; several chroniclers wrote versions years later, and they differ, though most report the crowd's cry of Deus vult, God wills it. Urban then toured France for months encouraging recruitment.

sections.h2: Bari, Jerusalem and Urban's Death
paras: In 1098 Urban held a council at Bari to discuss differences with the Greek Church, where St. Anselm of Canterbury defended the Western teaching on the procession of the Holy Spirit. The crusaders took Antioch in 1098 and Jerusalem on July 15, 1099, with great bloodshed.

Urban died in Rome on July 29, 1099, before news of Jerusalem's capture could reach him. He was beatified by Pope Leo XIII in 1881, and his feast is kept on July 29. The crusading movement he began remains one of the most debated legacies in Church history.

keyFacts: Born Odo of Châtillon (Lagery) in Champagne, around 1035
Reigned March 12, 1088 – July 29, 1099
Prior of Cluny; made cardinal bishop of Ostia by Gregory VII
Called the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont, November 1095
Held the Council of Bari (1098) with St. Anselm on the filioque
Beatified by Leo XIII in 1881

faqs.question: What did Urban II say at Clermont?
faqs.answer: He called on Western knights to aid Eastern Christians and liberate Jerusalem, offering remission of penance to those who went from devotion. The exact wording is unknown, since the surviving accounts were written later and differ from one another.

faqs.question: Did Urban II know that Jerusalem was captured?
faqs.answer: No. Crusaders took Jerusalem on July 15, 1099, and Urban died on July 29, before the news reached Rome.

faqs.question: Why was Urban II elected outside Rome?
faqs.answer: The antipope Clement III, supported by Henry IV, controlled Rome in 1088, so the cardinals met at Terracina to elect him.

directAnswer: Pope Paschal II was Ranierius, a monk and cardinal from central Italy who reigned from 1099 to 1118. His long pontificate saw a settlement of the investiture dispute in England, a dramatic confrontation in which Emperor Henry V imprisoned him and extracted concessions he later revoked, and papal approval of the Knights Hospitaller.

sections.h2: Ranierius, Cardinal of San Clemente
paras: Ranierius was born in the Romagna, near Santa Sofia, and entered monastic life young; which monastery he joined is uncertain. Gregory VII made him cardinal priest of San Clemente. Elected on August 13, 1099, two weeks after Urban II's death, he inherited a papacy strengthened by the First Crusade but still at odds with the German emperor.
After the death of the antipope Clement III in 1100, imperial partisans raised several short-lived successors, none of whom posed a serious threat.

sections.h2: Investiture Settled in England
paras: In England, Archbishop Anselm of Canterbury had refused to accept lay investiture from King Henry I. After lengthy negotiations, a settlement was reached in 1107: the king gave up investing bishops with ring and staff, while bishops would still do homage for their lands. The compromise anticipated the solution later reached with the empire.

sections.h2: Henry V, Sutri and the Pravilegium
paras: In 1111 Paschal proposed a radical bargain to Henry V: the emperor would renounce investiture, and German bishops would return to the crown the lands and rights they held from it. When the plan was read in St. Peter's during the coronation ceremony in February 1111, bishops and nobles erupted in protest. Henry seized the pope and cardinals and held them for about two months.

Under pressure, Paschal granted the emperor the right of investiture and crowned him on April 13, 1111. Reformers denounced the concession, mockingly called a pravilegium, and a Lateran synod in 1112 declared it void. The episode damaged Paschal's reputation but showed that the issue required a negotiated settlement.

sections.h2: The Hospitallers and Roman Churches
paras: In 1113 Paschal issued the bull Pie postulatio voluntatis, taking the Hospital of St. John in Jerusalem under papal protection and confirming its independence. This was a founding moment for the order later known as the Knights Hospitaller, today the Sovereign Military Order of Malta.

In Rome he rebuilt the church of Santi Quattro Coronati, consecrated in 1116, after the destruction of 1084. The present upper basilica of San Clemente also dates from his era, and tradition credits him with founding Santa Maria del Popolo. Expelled from Rome by unrest in 1117, he returned shortly before dying there on January 21, 1118.

keyFacts: Personal name: Ranierius; cardinal priest of San Clemente
Reigned August 13, 1099 – January 21, 1118
English investiture settlement with Henry I and St. Anselm (1107)
Imprisoned by Henry V in 1111; his forced concession was annulled in 1112
Bull Pie postulatio voluntatis (1113) recognized the Hospitallers
Rebuilt Santi Quattro Coronati, consecrated 1116

faqs.question: What happened between Paschal II and Henry V in 1111?
faqs.answer: After a proposed settlement collapsed at the coronation, Henry V took the pope and cardinals captive and forced Paschal to grant him the right of investiture. A Lateran synod in 1112 revoked the concession.

faqs.question: How is Paschal II connected to the Order of Malta?
faqs.answer: His 1113 bull Pie postulatio voluntatis took the Hospital of St. John in Jerusalem under papal protection, a key step in the formation of the Knights Hospitaller, later the Order of Malta.

faqs.question: How was investiture resolved in England under Paschal II?
faqs.answer: In 1107 King Henry I renounced investing bishops with ring and staff, while bishops continued to do homage for their temporal holdings.

directAnswer: Pope Gelasius II was John of Gaeta, a Monte Cassino monk who served as papal chancellor for about three decades before reigning for one turbulent year, 1118 to 1119. Attacked by the Frangipani family, driven from Rome by Emperor Henry V, and opposed by an imperial antipope, he died in exile at Cluny.

sections.h2: John of Gaeta, Chancellor of the Roman Church
paras: John was born at Gaeta and became a monk of Monte Cassino. Urban II brought him to Rome and made him chancellor, a post he held under Urban and Paschal II. He is credited with improving the Latin style of papal documents, including the rhythmic prose cadence known as the cursus, which gave papal letters a recognizable form.

sections.h2: Seized at His Election and Driven Into Exile
paras: Elected on January 24, 1118, he was immediately attacked by Cencius Frangipane and his armed followers, who broke into the meeting, beat the new pope and held him captive until the Romans forced his release. When Henry V approached Rome weeks later, Gelasius fled to Gaeta, where he was ordained priest and consecrated bishop.

Henry then had Maurice Bourdin, archbishop of Braga, set up as antipope Gregory VIII. Gelasius excommunicated both the emperor and the antipope. Returning to Rome, he was attacked again by the Frangipani in July 1118 while celebrating Mass and escaped only with difficulty.

He sailed for France, was received by Church leaders there, and died at the abbey of Cluny on January 29, 1119. Beyond these dramatic events and his long service as chancellor, the sources reveal little about his personal life.

keyFacts: Personal name: John of Gaeta
Reigned January 24, 1118 – January 29, 1119
Monk of Monte Cassino and papal chancellor under Urban II and Paschal II
Opposed by the imperial antipope Gregory VIII (Maurice Bourdin)
Died in exile at the abbey of Cluny

faqs.question: Why did Gelasius II die in France?
faqs.answer: Violence from the Frangipani family and pressure from Emperor Henry V made Rome unsafe, so he fled to France in 1118 and died at Cluny in January 1119.

faqs.question: What is Gelasius II remembered for before he became pope?
faqs.answer: As chancellor for roughly thirty years, he refined the style of papal documents, including the use of the rhythmic cursus in papal letters.

directAnswer: Pope Callixtus II was Guy of Burgundy, archbishop of Vienne and a member of the comital family of Burgundy, who reigned from 1119 to 1124. He ended the Investiture Controversy with the Concordat of Worms in 1122 and convened the First Lateran Council in 1123, the first ecumenical council held in the West.

sections.h2: Guy of Burgundy, Archbishop of Vienne
paras: Guy was a son of Count William I of Burgundy and was related to the royal houses of France, England and Germany. As archbishop of Vienne from 1088 he was a firm reformer. In 1112 he led a synod at Vienne that condemned the investiture privilege Henry V had forced from Paschal II, and excommunicated the emperor.

After Gelasius II died at Cluny, the cardinals who had accompanied him elected Guy there on February 2, 1119. The choice of a prelate with powerful family ties and a reputation for firmness proved decisive.

sections.h2: Ending the Antipope Gregory VIII's Challenge
paras: Callixtus entered Rome in 1120 to a warm reception. The imperial antipope Gregory VIII had retreated to Sutri, which papal forces captured in 1121. The antipope was publicly humiliated and confined in monasteries for the rest of his life. Callixtus also issued a bull, later known by its opening words Sicut Judaeis, forbidding Christians to harm Jews, force them to be baptized, or disturb their cemeteries.

sections.h2: The Concordat of Worms
paras: Negotiations with Henry V concluded at Worms on September 23, 1122. The emperor renounced investiture with ring and staff, the symbols of spiritual office, and guaranteed free canonical elections of bishops and abbots. The pope allowed elections in Germany to take place in the emperor's presence and permitted him to invest the elected candidate with the temporal rights of the office, signified by a scepter, before consecration; in Italy and Burgundy this was to follow consecration.
The compromise drew a distinction between the spiritual and temporal sides of a bishop's office and closed a conflict that had begun under Gregory VII nearly fifty years earlier.

sections.h2: The First Lateran Council
paras: In March 1123 Callixtus convened a council at the Lateran, counted as the ninth ecumenical council and the first held in the West. It confirmed the Concordat of Worms, renewed decrees against simony and against marriage and concubinage among clergy in major orders, upheld the Truce of God, and protected the property and families of crusaders.
Callixtus died in Rome on December 13, 1124.

keyFacts: Personal name: Guy of Burgundy, archbishop of Vienne
Reigned February 2, 1119 – December 13, 1124; elected at Cluny
Concordat of Worms with Henry V (September 23, 1122)
Convened the First Lateran Council (1123), the ninth ecumenical council
Captured the antipope Gregory VIII at Sutri (1121)
Issued a bull protecting Jews, known as Sicut Judaeis

faqs.question: What did the Concordat of Worms decide?
faqs.answer: The emperor gave up investing bishops with ring and staff and guaranteed free elections, while the pope allowed the emperor to confer the temporal rights of the office with a scepter. It ended the Investiture Controversy in 1122.

faqs.question: Why was the First Lateran Council important?
faqs.answer: Held in 1123, it was the first ecumenical council in the West. It ratified the Concordat of Worms and renewed reform decrees on simony and clerical celibacy.

faqs.question: Where was Callixtus II elected?
faqs.answer: At the abbey of Cluny in France, on February 2, 1119, by the cardinals who had accompanied the exiled Gelasius II.

directAnswer: Pope Honorius II was Lamberto Scannabecchi, cardinal bishop of Ostia and one of the negotiators of the Concordat of Worms, who reigned from 1124 to 1130. Elected amid pressure from the Frangipani family, he approved the Premonstratensians, saw the Knights Templar receive their rule, and contended with Roger II over southern Italy.

sections.h2: Lamberto of Fiagnano and the Concordat of Worms
paras: Lamberto was born of modest family at Fiagnano, in the territory of Casalfiumanese near Imola. He became a canon regular, archdeacon of Bologna, and later cardinal bishop of Ostia. Callixtus II sent him to Germany as legate, and he was one of the papal negotiators who concluded the Concordat of Worms in 1122.

sections.h2: A Contested Election in 1124
paras: When Callixtus II died in December 1124, a group of cardinals chose Cardinal Theobald Boccapecci, who took the name Celestine. Before he could be installed, Robert Frangipane and his armed supporters forced the acclamation of Lamberto instead. Theobald stepped aside to avoid bloodshed.

Uneasy about the irregular way he had been chosen, Lamberto resigned a few days later before the cardinals, who then elected him again. The episode revealed rivalries between Roman families, especially the Frangipani and the Pierleoni, that would split the Church at his death.

sections.h2: New Orders: Premonstratensians and Templars
paras: In 1126 Honorius approved the Order of Canons Regular founded by St. Norbert at Prémontré. Two years later, at the Council of Troyes, held in January 1129 by modern reckoning and attended by his legate, the Knights Templar received a formal rule; St. Bernard of Clairvaux was closely involved. This recognition made the Templars the first military religious order with a written rule approved by the Church.

sections.h2: Lothair III and Roger II of Sicily
paras: In Germany Honorius recognized the election of Lothair III in 1125, supporting him against the Hohenstaufen claimant Conrad. In southern Italy he tried to stop Roger II of Sicily from taking over the duchy of Apulia, even preaching a campaign against him, but in 1128 he was forced to invest Roger as duke.
Honorius died in Rome on February 13, 1130. His death set off the schism between Innocent II and Anacletus II.

keyFacts: Personal name: Lamberto Scannabecchi, cardinal bishop of Ostia
Reigned December 15, 1124 – February 13, 1130
Papal negotiator of the Concordat of Worms (1122)
Approved St. Norbert's Premonstratensian canons (1126)
The Knights Templar received their rule at the Council of Troyes in the late 1120s
Invested Roger II as duke of Apulia (1128)

faqs.question: Why did Honorius II resign right after his election?
faqs.answer: He had been forced into office by the Frangipani over a candidate the cardinals had already chosen. To resolve doubts, he resigned before the cardinals, who promptly elected him again.

faqs.question: Did Honorius II approve the Knights Templar?
faqs.answer: The Templars received their rule at the Council of Troyes during his pontificate, with his legate present and St. Bernard of Clairvaux closely involved.

faqs.question: Which religious order founded by St. Norbert did Honorius II approve?
faqs.answer: In 1126 he approved the Premonstratensian canons, also called Norbertines, founded at Prémontré.

directAnswer: Pope Innocent II was Gregorio Papareschi, a Roman cardinal who reigned from 1130 to 1143. Elected in a divided vote that produced the rival claimant Anacletus II, he won recognition across Europe with the help of St. Bernard of Clairvaux, ended the schism, and convened the Second Lateran Council in 1139.

sections.h2: Gregorio Papareschi and the Double Election of 1130
paras: Gregorio came from the Trastevere district of Rome and served as cardinal deacon of Sant'Angelo. He was among the legates who negotiated the Concordat of Worms. When Honorius II died on the night of February 13–14, 1130, a group of cardinals allied with the chancellor Haimeric and the Frangipani family hurriedly elected Gregorio as Innocent II.

Later the same day a larger number of cardinals elected Pietro Pierleoni, who took the name Anacletus II. Both claimed legitimacy, and the Church was divided for eight years. Anacletus held most of Rome, and Innocent left for France.

sections.h2: Bernard of Clairvaux and the Recognition of Europe
paras: At the Council of Étampes in 1130, St. Bernard of Clairvaux argued that Innocent was the worthier candidate, and France accepted him. Henry I of England and Lothair III of Germany followed. Anacletus found his main ally in Roger II, whom he crowned king of Sicily in 1130.

Lothair escorted Innocent to Rome, and in 1133 Innocent crowned him emperor in the Lateran, since St. Peter's remained in Anacletus's hands. The schism ended when Anacletus died in January 1138 and his successor submitted to Innocent shortly afterward.

sections.h2: The Second Lateran Council
paras: In April 1139 Innocent convened the Second Lateran Council, counted as the tenth ecumenical council. It annulled the acts of Anacletus, deposed clergy he had ordained, and declared that marriages attempted by clerics in major orders and by professed religious were not merely forbidden but invalid. Other canons condemned simony, usury and the teachings of certain heretics, and one canon prohibited the use of crossbows and bows against Christians.
The council also condemned Arnold of Brescia, a reforming preacher who attacked clerical wealth, and in 1140 or 1141 Innocent confirmed the condemnation of Peter Abelard after the Council of Sens.

sections.h2: Defeat by Roger II and Final Years
paras: Weeks after the council, Innocent led troops against Roger II, was captured at Galluccio in July 1139, and was forced to recognize him as king of Sicily in the Treaty of Mignano. In Rome he rebuilt the basilica of Santa Maria in Trastevere, whose apse mosaic shows him holding a model of the church.
In his final year the citizens of Rome rose against papal government and established a commune. Innocent died on September 24, 1143.

keyFacts: Personal name: Gregorio Papareschi, of Rome
Reigned February 14, 1130 – September 24, 1143
Rival claimant Anacletus II divided the Church from 1130 to 1138
Supported by St. Bernard of Clairvaux at the Council of Étampes (1130)
Convened the Second Lateran Council (1139), the tenth ecumenical council
Rebuilt Santa Maria in Trastevere

faqs.question: Who was Anacletus II?
faqs.answer: Pietro Pierleoni was elected by a larger group of cardinals on the same day as Innocent II in 1130. The Church eventually recognized Innocent, and Anacletus is counted as an antipope.

faqs.question: What did the Second Lateran Council decide?
faqs.answer: Held in 1139, it annulled Anacletus II's acts, declared marriages attempted by clerics in major orders invalid, condemned simony and usury, and banned the use of crossbows and bows against Christians.

faqs.question: How did St. Bernard help Innocent II?
faqs.answer: Bernard championed Innocent's cause at the Council of Étampes and across Europe, persuading rulers and bishops to recognize him rather than Anacletus II.

directAnswer: Pope Celestine II was Guido of Città di Castello, a learned cardinal and former student of Peter Abelard, who reigned for about five months, from September 1143 to March 1144. His main recorded act was lifting the interdict Innocent II had placed on the lands of King Louis VII of France.

sections.h2: Guido of Città di Castello, Scholar and Cardinal
paras: Guido came from Città di Castello in Umbria. He studied under Peter Abelard in France and was regarded as one of the most educated members of the Roman Curia. He was made a cardinal and served as a papal legate before his election on September 26, 1143.

Medieval writers note that he remained on friendly terms with Abelard's circle even after Abelard's condemnation, and he is said to have owned copies of his teacher's works. Beyond that, little is known of his personal life.

sections.h2: Peace With Louis VII
paras: Innocent II had placed France under an interdict after Louis VII opposed the pope's candidate for the archbishopric of Bourges. One of Celestine's first acts was to lift that interdict, restoring normal sacramental life in the king's lands. He also had to deal with the newly formed Roman Commune, which had rejected papal rule over the city shortly before his election.

Celestine died on March 8, 1144. In later centuries he gained an unexpected kind of fame: the so-called Prophecy of St. Malachy, a list of mottoes for popes first published in 1595 and widely regarded by historians as a sixteenth-century composition, begins with him.

keyFacts: Personal name: Guido of Città di Castello
Reigned September 26, 1143 – March 8, 1144
A former student of Peter Abelard
Lifted the interdict on the lands of Louis VII of France
First pope named in the so-called Prophecy of St. Malachy, published in 1595

faqs.question: Was Celestine II a student of Abelard?
faqs.answer: Yes. Guido studied under Peter Abelard and remained sympathetic to his teacher's circle, even after Abelard's condemnation.

faqs.question: What is Celestine II's connection to the Prophecy of St. Malachy?
faqs.answer: That list of mottoes for future popes begins with him. It first appeared in print in 1595, and most historians consider it a sixteenth-century composition rather than a genuine work of St. Malachy.

directAnswer: Pope Lucius II was Gherardo Caccianemici of Bologna, a canon regular and papal chancellor who reigned for less than a year, from March 1144 to February 1145. His pontificate was dominated by the struggle with the new Roman Commune, which had taken over government of the city.

sections.h2: Gherardo of Bologna, Canon and Chancellor
paras: Gherardo was born in Bologna and became a canon regular, associated with the community of San Frediano in Lucca. He was made a cardinal and served as papal legate in Germany several times and as chancellor and librarian of the Roman Church under Celestine II.

sections.h2: Confronting the Roman Commune
paras: Shortly before his election, the citizens of Rome had rebelled against papal government, revived the ancient Senate on the Capitoline Hill, and later chose Giordano Pierleoni as patrician. Lucius refused to accept the commune and sought help from King Roger II of Sicily and from the German king Conrad III, but neither gave effective support. He also had to settle disputes with Roger over territory in southern Italy.

Lucius died on February 15, 1145. According to a chronicle written some decades later, he was struck by a stone while leading an attack on the Capitol and died of his injuries; contemporary sources do not confirm this, so historians treat the story with caution. Apart from these struggles, little is recorded of his brief reign.

keyFacts: Personal name: Gherardo Caccianemici of Bologna
Reigned March 9, 1144 – February 15, 1145
Canon regular linked to San Frediano in Lucca
Papal legate in Germany and chancellor before his election
Opposed the Roman Commune and its revived Senate

faqs.question: Was Lucius II killed during a battle in Rome?
faqs.answer: A later chronicle says he was mortally wounded by a stone while attacking the Capitol, but earlier sources do not confirm it. The cause of his death is therefore uncertain.

faqs.question: What was the Roman Commune that Lucius II opposed?
faqs.answer: It was a citizens' government formed in 1143–1144 that revived the Roman Senate and rejected the pope's temporal rule over the city.

directAnswer: Blessed Eugene III was Bernardo of Pisa, a Cistercian monk and disciple of St. Bernard of Clairvaux, who reigned from 1145 to 1153. He proclaimed the Second Crusade, spent much of his pontificate in exile from rebellious Rome, and encouraged the visionary writings of St. Hildegard of Bingen.

sections.h2: A Monk of Clairvaux on the Chair of Peter
paras: Bernardo was born near Pisa and served in the cathedral clergy there. After meeting St. Bernard, he became a Cistercian monk at Clairvaux, and in 1140 he was sent to Rome as abbot of the monastery of Sts. Vincent and Anastasius at Tre Fontane.

When Lucius II died, the cardinals elected him on February 15, 1145, the same day. He was not a cardinal, and his election surprised many, including St. Bernard, who wrote with some alarm that a simple monk had been made pope. Bernard later addressed his treatise De consideratione to Eugene, offering advice on the spiritual dangers of papal office.

sections.h2: Exile From Rome and Arnold of Brescia
paras: The Roman Commune refused to accept the new pope's temporal authority, and Eugene left the city within days to be consecrated at the abbey of Farfa. For most of his pontificate he lived away from Rome, in Viterbo, in France and elsewhere, returning only for short periods.

The reforming preacher Arnold of Brescia came to Rome during these years and supported the commune, denouncing clerical wealth. In 1153, shortly before his death, Eugene concluded the Treaty of Constance with Frederick Barbarossa, in which the king promised to help restore papal authority in Rome.

sections.h2: Quantum praedecessores and the Second Crusade
paras: The fall of the crusader county of Edessa in 1144 prompted Eugene to issue the bull Quantum praedecessores on December 1, 1145, reissued in 1146. It called for a new crusade and set out spiritual and legal privileges for those who took the cross. He entrusted the preaching to St. Bernard, who launched the effort at Vézelay in 1146.

Louis VII of France and Conrad III of Germany led armies east, but the crusade failed, especially after the abandoned siege of Damascus in 1148. Its collapse was a deep disappointment to Eugene and Bernard.

sections.h2: Hildegard, Reims and Eugene's Beatification
paras: During a synod at Trier in 1147–1148, Eugene read from the early writings of Hildegard of Bingen and encouraged her to continue recording her visions, a significant endorsement for a woman writer of her time. At the Council of Reims in 1148 he presided over the examination of the theologian Gilbert of Poitiers and renewed reform decrees.
Eugene died at Tivoli on July 8, 1153, and was buried in St. Peter's. Pope Pius IX beatified him in 1872.

keyFacts: Personal name: Bernardo of Pisa; Cistercian monk of Clairvaux
Reigned February 15, 1145 – July 8, 1153
Issued Quantum praedecessores (1145) proclaiming the Second Crusade
St. Bernard addressed De consideratione to him
Encouraged the writings of St. Hildegard of Bingen (1147–1148)
Beatified by Pius IX in 1872

faqs.question: What was Eugene III's relationship with St. Bernard of Clairvaux?
faqs.answer: Eugene had been Bernard's monk at Clairvaux. As pope he entrusted Bernard with preaching the Second Crusade, and Bernard wrote De consideratione to guide him in his office.

faqs.question: Why did Eugene III live outside Rome?
faqs.answer: The Roman Commune rejected papal government of the city, so Eugene spent most of his pontificate in Viterbo, France and other places.

faqs.question: How did Eugene III support Hildegard of Bingen?
faqs.answer: At the synod of Trier in 1147–1148 he read from her writings and encouraged her to continue writing down her visions.

directAnswer: Pope Anastasius IV was Corrado della Suburra, an elderly Roman cardinal bishop of Sabina who reigned for about seventeen months, from July 1153 to December 1154. Known for a conciliatory approach, he settled several disputes, including the long contest over the archbishopric of York.

sections.h2: Corrado della Suburra, Guardian of Rome
paras: Corrado was a Roman, born in the Suburra district, and was already advanced in years when elected. As cardinal bishop of Sabina, he had remained in Rome as papal vicar while Innocent II was in exile in France during the schism of Anacletus II, giving him long experience of the city's factions. He was elected on July 8, 1153, the day Eugene III died.

sections.h2: A Reign of Reconciliation
paras: Unlike his predecessor, Anastasius was able to live in Rome, apparently by maintaining an accommodation with the commune. He took a moderate line with Frederick Barbarossa, accepting the transfer of Bishop Wichmann to the archbishopric of Magdeburg, which Eugene III had resisted.

In England he ended the dispute over York by granting the pallium to William FitzHerbert, whom earlier popes had deposed; William is venerated today as St. William of York. In 1154 he confirmed and expanded the privileges of the Knights Hospitaller.

Anastasius died on December 3, 1154, and was buried in the Lateran in a porphyry sarcophagus traditionally said to have held the remains of St. Helena. The surviving record of his pontificate is limited to such acts.

keyFacts: Personal name: Corrado della Suburra, cardinal bishop of Sabina
Reigned July 8, 1153 – December 3, 1154
Served as papal vicar in Rome during Innocent II's exile
Granted the pallium to William FitzHerbert of York (St. William)
Buried in the porphyry sarcophagus associated with St. Helena

faqs.question: How did Anastasius IV resolve the dispute over York?
faqs.answer: He restored William FitzHerbert as archbishop of York and gave him the pallium. William died soon after and was later venerated as St. William of York.

faqs.question: Why is Anastasius IV considered a conciliatory pope?
faqs.answer: He avoided confrontation with the Roman Commune and with Frederick Barbarossa, accepting compromises on contested appointments that Eugene III had opposed.

directAnswer: Pope Adrian IV was Nicholas Breakspear, the only Englishman to serve as pope, who reigned from 1154 to 1159. A former abbot and papal legate to Scandinavia, he crowned Frederick Barbarossa emperor, placed Rome under interdict to expel Arnold of Brescia, and is linked to the disputed bull Laudabiliter concerning Ireland.

sections.h2: Nicholas Breakspear, From Hertfordshire to Saint-Ruf
paras: Nicholas was born around 1100 in Hertfordshire, according to tradition near Abbots Langley. As a young man he went to France and joined the canons regular of Saint-Ruf near Avignon, where he was eventually elected abbot. Complaints from some of his canons brought him to the attention of Eugene III, who made him cardinal bishop of Albano around 1149.

sections.h2: Legate to Norway and Sweden
paras: In 1152 Eugene sent him as legate to Scandinavia. He reorganized the Church in Norway, establishing the archdiocese of Nidaros (Trondheim) in 1153 with authority over Norway and the Atlantic islands, and held a council in Sweden that prepared the way for a Swedish archbishopric. His work there earned him lasting respect in the North. On his return he was elected pope on December 4, 1154.

sections.h2: Arnold of Brescia and the Interdict on Rome
paras: The Roman Commune, inspired by Arnold of Brescia, continued to defy papal rule. After a cardinal was attacked in the street, Adrian placed the city of Rome under interdict in 1155, the first time this had happened. With the churches closed during Holy Week, the Romans expelled Arnold. He was later captured and handed over to the city prefect, who had him executed in 1155.

sections.h2: Frederick Barbarossa and the Besançon Incident
paras: Adrian crowned Frederick Barbarossa emperor in St. Peter's on June 18, 1155, after a tense dispute at their first meeting over whether the king would perform the ceremonial service of holding the pope's stirrup. Relations soured when Adrian made peace with William I of Sicily in the Treaty of Benevento in 1156.

At the Diet of Besançon in 1157, a papal letter describing the empire as a beneficium conferred by the pope was translated as fief, provoking outrage among the German princes. Adrian later explained he had meant a benefit or good deed, not a feudal grant, but the mistrust endured.

sections.h2: Laudabiliter and Ireland
paras: Adrian is associated with Laudabiliter, a bull said to have approved Henry II of England's intervention in Ireland in order to reform its Church. Its text survives only through the writings of Gerald of Wales, and historians still debate whether it is genuine, altered, or a later fabrication. John of Salisbury, a friend of the pope, recorded that Adrian granted Ireland to Henry, though the exact nature of the grant is uncertain.
Adrian died at Anagni on September 1, 1159, and was buried in St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Born Nicholas Breakspear in Hertfordshire around 1100
Reigned December 4, 1154 – September 1, 1159
The only English pope; abbot of the canons regular of Saint-Ruf
As legate, established the archdiocese of Nidaros (Trondheim) in 1153
Crowned Frederick Barbarossa emperor on June 18, 1155
Linked to the disputed bull Laudabiliter on Ireland

faqs.question: Was Adrian IV the only English pope?
faqs.answer: Yes. Nicholas Breakspear of Hertfordshire is the only pope born in England.

faqs.question: Did Adrian IV really give Ireland to Henry II?
faqs.answer: Contemporaries such as John of Salisbury say he made some grant, but the bull Laudabiliter survives only in Gerald of Wales's writings, and historians debate its authenticity and content.

faqs.question: Why did Adrian IV put Rome under interdict?
faqs.answer: In 1155 he used the interdict to pressure the Romans into expelling Arnold of Brescia, whose movement backed the Roman Commune against papal rule.

directAnswer: Pope Alexander III was Rolando of Siena, papal chancellor under Eugene III and Adrian IV, who reigned from 1159 to 1181. He withstood an eighteen-year schism backed by Frederick Barbarossa, reconciled with the emperor at the Peace of Venice in 1177, canonized St. Thomas Becket, and convened the Third Lateran Council in 1179.

sections.h2: Rolando of Siena, Chancellor of the Roman Church
paras: Rolando was born in Siena; the family name Bandinelli, often given to him, is doubted by modern historians, as is his identification with the canon lawyer Rolandus of Bologna. Eugene III made him a cardinal, and he became chancellor of the Roman Church in 1153, serving as Adrian IV's chief adviser.
He was among the legates at the Diet of Besançon in 1157, where the dispute over papal language describing the empire set him at odds with Frederick Barbarossa.

sections.h2: The Schism of 1159 and Eighteen Years of Struggle
paras: On September 7, 1159, most cardinals elected Rolando. A pro-imperial minority chose Cardinal Octavian, who took the name Victor IV, and Frederick backed him. After Victor's death the imperial side named successors, Paschal III and Callixtus III, prolonging the division.

Alexander won the recognition of France, England, Sicily and most of Western Christendom, but he spent the years 1162 to 1165 in exile in France. He allied with the cities of the Lombard League, which defeated Frederick at the Battle of Legnano in 1176. In the Peace of Venice in 1177, Frederick recognized Alexander as pope and made public reverence to him at St. Mark's.

sections.h2: Thomas Becket and Henry II
paras: Alexander supported Archbishop Thomas Becket of Canterbury in his conflict with King Henry II over the rights of the Church, though he sometimes urged caution because he needed English support against the emperor. After Becket was murdered in his cathedral in December 1170, Alexander canonized him in 1173. Henry did penance and reached a settlement with papal legates at Avranches in 1172.
Alexander also canonized St. Bernard of Clairvaux in 1174, and in 1179 his bull Manifestis probatum recognized Afonso Henriques as king of Portugal.

sections.h2: The Third Lateran Council
paras: In March 1179 Alexander convened the Third Lateran Council, counted as the eleventh ecumenical council. Its first canon, Licet de vitanda, required a two-thirds majority of the cardinals for a valid papal election, a rule meant to prevent schisms like the one he had endured, and still the basis of papal elections today. Other canons set minimum ages for bishops, condemned the Cathars, and required each cathedral to support a master to teach clerics and poor students without charge.
Alexander died at Civita Castellana on August 30, 1181. His long reign also produced a large body of decretal letters that became foundational for medieval canon law.

keyFacts: Personal name: Rolando of Siena; papal chancellor from 1153
Reigned September 7, 1159 – August 30, 1181
Opposed by imperial antipopes Victor IV, Paschal III and Callixtus III
Peace of Venice with Frederick Barbarossa (1177)
Canonized St. Thomas Becket (1173) and St. Bernard of Clairvaux (1174)
Third Lateran Council (1179) set the two-thirds rule for papal elections

faqs.question: Why did the Third Lateran Council require a two-thirds majority?
faqs.answer: Alexander III had faced an eighteen-year schism after a divided election in 1159. The canon Licet de vitanda required two-thirds of the cardinals to agree, making a rival election far harder.

faqs.question: What was Alexander III's role in the Becket affair?
faqs.answer: He supported Becket against Henry II, while trying to keep English backing in his struggle with the emperor, and he canonized Becket in 1173, little more than two years after the archbishop's murder.

faqs.question: How did Alexander III's conflict with Frederick Barbarossa end?
faqs.answer: After the Lombard League defeated Frederick at Legnano in 1176, the emperor recognized Alexander in the Peace of Venice in 1177.

directAnswer: Pope Lucius III was Ubaldo Allucingoli of Lucca, cardinal bishop of Ostia, who reigned from 1181 to 1185. Spending most of his pontificate away from Rome, he met Frederick Barbarossa at Verona and issued the decree Ad abolendam against heresy, an early step toward the medieval inquisition.

sections.h2: Ubaldo of Lucca, Veteran of the Curia
paras: Ubaldo was born in Lucca and served in the Curia for decades. He was made a cardinal in the time of Innocent II and later became cardinal bishop of Ostia. A trusted diplomat under Alexander III, he took part in negotiations with Frederick Barbarossa that led to the Peace of Venice. He was elected on September 1, 1181, apparently the first pope chosen under the two-thirds rule of the Third Lateran Council.

sections.h2: Verona and the Decree Ad abolendam
paras: Conflict with the Roman Commune soon drove Lucius from the city, and he spent most of his reign elsewhere. In 1184 he met Frederick at Verona. There, in November 1184, the decree Ad abolendam condemned the Cathars, the Waldensians, the Humiliati and other groups, and instructed bishops to inquire regularly into heresy in their dioceses, with those convicted handed over to secular authorities for punishment. Historians see it as a forerunner of later inquisitorial procedures.

Talks with Frederick on other issues, including the lands of Countess Matilda of Tuscany and the imperial coronation of Frederick's son Henry, ended without agreement. Lucius died at Verona on November 25, 1185, and was buried in its cathedral. Little is recorded of his personal life beyond his long curial career.

keyFacts: Personal name: Ubaldo Allucingoli of Lucca
Reigned September 1, 1181 – November 25, 1185
Cardinal bishop of Ostia; negotiator of the Peace of Venice
Issued Ad abolendam against heresy at Verona (1184)
Died and was buried at Verona

faqs.question: What was the decree Ad abolendam?
faqs.answer: Issued at Verona in 1184 with Frederick Barbarossa's support, it condemned several heretical movements and required bishops to investigate heresy in their dioceses, foreshadowing the later inquisition.

faqs.question: Why did Lucius III live outside Rome?
faqs.answer: Disputes with the Roman Commune forced him to leave the city, and he spent most of his pontificate in other Italian cities, finally at Verona.

directAnswer: Pope Urban III was Uberto Crivelli, archbishop of Milan, who reigned from November 1185 to October 1187. Elected at Verona, he spent his short pontificate in a bitter dispute with Emperor Frederick Barbarossa and his son Henry VI, and died at Ferrara as news of the crusader defeat at Hattin was reaching Europe.

sections.h2: Uberto Crivelli of Milan
paras: Uberto was born at Cuggiono, near Milan, into the Crivelli family. He was made a cardinal and became archbishop of Milan in 1185. Elected pope at Verona on November 25, 1185, the day Lucius III died, he kept the archbishopric of Milan, a city that had suffered greatly at Frederick Barbarossa's hands, which helps explain his firm stance toward the emperor.

sections.h2: Quarrels With Frederick and Henry VI
paras: In January 1186 Frederick's son Henry married Constance, heiress of the Kingdom of Sicily, in Milan, a union that threatened to surround the Papal States with Hohenstaufen power. Urban refused to crown Henry as co-emperor. He also consecrated Folmar as archbishop of Trier against the emperor's wishes, and Henry's troops responded by occupying parts of the Papal States. German bishops largely sided with the emperor.

Urban was preparing to excommunicate Frederick when he died at Ferrara on October 20, 1187. Some chroniclers say grief over the defeat of the crusader army at Hattin in July 1187 hastened his death, though that account cannot be verified. He was buried in Ferrara Cathedral.

keyFacts: Personal name: Uberto Crivelli, archbishop of Milan
Born at Cuggiono near Milan
Reigned November 25, 1185 – October 20, 1187
Refused to crown Henry VI as co-emperor
Died at Ferrara and buried in its cathedral

faqs.question: Why did Urban III clash with Frederick Barbarossa?
faqs.answer: He resisted the marriage alliance linking the Hohenstaufen to Sicily, refused to crown Henry VI as co-emperor, and consecrated an archbishop of Trier the emperor opposed.

faqs.question: Did Urban III die of grief over Hattin?
faqs.answer: Some medieval chroniclers say so, but it cannot be confirmed. He died at Ferrara in October 1187, a few months after the battle.

directAnswer: Pope Gregory VIII was Alberto de Morra of Benevento, chancellor of the Roman Church under Alexander III, who reigned for less than two months in late 1187. Elected days after news of the fall of Jerusalem reached the West, he issued the bull Audita tremendi calling for the Third Crusade and died at Pisa while trying to make peace between Pisa and Genoa.

sections.h2: Alberto de Morra, Jurist and Chancellor
paras: Alberto was born at Benevento and taught law before entering the service of the Curia. Adrian IV made him a cardinal, and he carried out legations for Alexander III, including to England in the aftermath of Thomas Becket's murder, where he helped arrange Henry II's reconciliation with the Church. In 1178 he became chancellor of the Roman Church, a post he held under Lucius III and Urban III.
Contemporaries described him as learned and personally austere. Some sources link him with the canons regular, though the details are uncertain.

sections.h2: Hattin, Jerusalem and the Election of 1187
paras: In July 1187 Saladin's army destroyed the forces of the Kingdom of Jerusalem at the Battle of Hattin and captured the relic of the True Cross carried into battle. Jerusalem itself surrendered on October 2. Urban III died at Ferrara on October 20, and the cardinals elected Alberto the next day, October 21, 1187.

sections.h2: Audita tremendi and the Call to Crusade
paras: Within days, on October 29, 1187, Gregory issued the bull Audita tremendi. It described the disaster in the East, interpreted it as a call to repentance for the sins of Christians, and summoned the faithful to take the cross, promising a plenary remission of penance to those who went with contrite hearts and protecting their property and families while they were away. He also ordered prayers and penitential fasting throughout Christendom.

The bull launched the Third Crusade, which drew Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, King Philip II of France and King Richard I of England. Its tone of penitence, rather than triumph, became a model for later crusade appeals.

sections.h2: Peacemaking and Death at Pisa
paras: Gregory sought to end the quarrels that had divided Urban III and the Hohenstaufen, adopting a conciliatory tone toward Henry VI, since the crusade required cooperation among Christian rulers. He traveled to Pisa to reconcile the rival maritime republics of Pisa and Genoa, whose fleets were needed to carry crusaders east.

He fell ill there and died on December 17, 1187, having reigned fifty-seven days. He was buried in Pisa Cathedral. His brief pontificate is remembered almost entirely for the crusade appeal that his successor, Clement III, carried forward.

keyFacts: Personal name: Alberto de Morra, of Benevento
Reigned October 21 – December 17, 1187
Chancellor of the Roman Church from 1178
Issued Audita tremendi (October 29, 1187) calling the Third Crusade
Died at Pisa while mediating between Pisa and Genoa

faqs.question: What was the bull Audita tremendi?
faqs.answer: Issued by Gregory VIII on October 29, 1187, after the defeat at Hattin and the loss of Jerusalem, it called Christians to repentance and to the Third Crusade, offering spiritual and legal privileges to crusaders.

faqs.question: Why did Gregory VIII go to Pisa?
faqs.answer: He went to make peace between Pisa and Genoa, whose ships were essential for transporting crusaders, and he died there in December 1187.

faqs.question: What role did Gregory VIII play in the Becket affair?
faqs.answer: As a cardinal legate he was among those sent to England after Thomas Becket's murder and helped negotiate King Henry II's reconciliation with the Church.

directAnswer: Pope Clement III was Paolo Scolari, a Roman and cardinal bishop of Palestrina, who reigned from December 1187 to March 1191. He made peace with the Roman Commune, allowing the papacy to return to Rome, and promoted the Third Crusade launched by his predecessor.

sections.h2: Paolo Scolari and the Return to Rome
paras: Paolo was a Roman by birth and served as cardinal bishop of Palestrina. He was elected at Pisa on December 19, 1187, two days after the death of Gregory VIII. Because he was a native Roman, he was well placed to settle the long feud between the popes and the Roman Commune, which had kept several of his predecessors in exile.

In 1188 he concluded a treaty with the Roman Senate: the city recognized papal sovereignty, while the pope accepted the Senate's existence and agreed to make annual payments to the city's officials. With this agreement the papacy returned to Rome after years of absence.

sections.h2: The Third Crusade and the Sicilian Question
paras: Clement worked to carry out Gregory VIII's crusade call, encouraging Frederick Barbarossa, Philip II of France and Richard I of England to take the cross and trying to settle disputes between the French and English kings. Frederick set out in 1189 but drowned in Asia Minor in 1190.

He also improved relations with the Hohenstaufen and agreed to crown Henry VI emperor. When William II of Sicily died in 1189, however, the papacy favored Tancred of Lecce as king rather than Henry's wife Constance, the legitimate heiress, a choice that set up conflict for his successor. Clement died in March 1191, shortly before Henry's arrival in Rome. Little is recorded of him beyond these political matters.

keyFacts: Personal name: Paolo Scolari, of Rome
Reigned December 19, 1187 – March 20, 1191
Cardinal bishop of Palestrina; elected at Pisa
Treaty with the Roman Senate (1188) returned the papacy to Rome
Promoted the Third Crusade

faqs.question: How did Clement III end the papal exile from Rome?
faqs.answer: In 1188 he reached a treaty with the Roman Senate in which the city acknowledged papal sovereignty and the pope recognized the Senate, allowing him to live in Rome.

faqs.question: What did Clement III do for the Third Crusade?
faqs.answer: He promoted the crusade proclaimed by Gregory VIII and worked to reconcile the kings of France and England so they could take part.

directAnswer: Pope Celestine III was Giacinto Bobone of Rome, who served as a cardinal deacon for about forty-seven years before being elected pope at roughly eighty-five. Reigning from 1191 to 1198, he crowned Emperor Henry VI, excommunicated Duke Leopold of Austria for imprisoning King Richard I, and defended the marriage of Queen Ingeborg of France.

sections.h2: Giacinto Bobone, Defender of Abelard
paras: Giacinto came from the Roman Bobone family, ancestors of the Orsini. As a young cleric he studied under Peter Abelard and spoke in his defense at the Council of Sens in 1140, a stance that earned him a rebuke from St. Bernard. He was made cardinal deacon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin in 1144 and served many popes, including as legate to Spain.
Elected on March 30, 1191, while still a deacon, he was ordained priest and consecrated bishop in mid-April. His motto, taken from the Psalms, asked God to guide his steps in the right paths.

sections.h2: Henry VI, Richard the Lionheart and Ingeborg
paras: The day after his consecration, Celestine crowned Henry VI and Constance as emperor and empress. Henry's ambitions in southern Italy, culminating in his conquest of Sicily in 1194, left the Papal States surrounded by imperial power, and Celestine avoided open confrontation.

When Duke Leopold V of Austria captured Richard I of England returning from crusade in 1192 and handed him over to Henry, Celestine excommunicated Leopold for seizing a crusader under the Church's protection. He also rejected the annulment Philip II of France had obtained from French bishops to set aside Queen Ingeborg of Denmark, declaring the marriage still valid. He took the German hospital brotherhood at Acre, forerunner of the Teutonic Knights, under papal protection.
Some contemporaries report that in his last days he wished to resign and name a successor, but the cardinals would not allow it. He died on January 8, 1198, and Innocent III was elected the same day.

keyFacts: Personal name: Giacinto Bobone, of Rome
Reigned March 30, 1191 – January 8, 1198
Cardinal deacon from 1144; elected at about eighty-five
Defended Peter Abelard at the Council of Sens (1140)
Crowned Henry VI emperor in April 1191
Excommunicated Leopold V of Austria over the captivity of Richard I

faqs.question: Why did Celestine III excommunicate Duke Leopold of Austria?
faqs.answer: Leopold captured King Richard I of England as he returned from the Third Crusade. Crusaders were under the Church's protection, so Celestine excommunicated him.

faqs.question: How old was Celestine III when elected?
faqs.answer: He was about eighty-five, one of the oldest men ever elected pope, after roughly forty-seven years as a cardinal deacon.

directAnswer: Pope Innocent III was Lotario dei Conti di Segni, elected at about thirty-seven, who reigned from 1198 to 1216 and is widely seen as the most powerful of the medieval popes.
