He intervened in the politics of the empire, England and France, called the Fourth Crusade and the Albigensian Crusade, welcomed St. Francis and St. Dominic, and convened the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215.

sections.h2: Lotario of Segni, Theologian and Canonist
paras: Lotario was born around 1160 at Gavignano, near Segni, into the family of the counts of Segni. He studied theology at Paris and law at Bologna, and his uncle Clement III made him a cardinal deacon. During the reign of Celestine III he wrote several works, including the treatise On the Misery of the Human Condition, a meditation on human frailty that circulated widely.
Elected on January 8, 1198, the day Celestine died, he was then only about thirty-seven and still a deacon.

sections.h2: Kings, Emperors and the Vicar of Christ
paras: Innocent described the pope as the Vicar of Christ and compared papal and royal authority to the sun and the moon. In the disputed German election after Henry VI's death, his bull Venerabilem (1202) asserted the pope's right to examine the candidate he would crown as emperor. He also acted as guardian of the young Frederick II, Henry's heir in Sicily.

When King John of England refused to accept Stephen Langton as archbishop of Canterbury, Innocent placed England under interdict in 1208 and later excommunicated John. In 1213 John submitted and made England a papal fief. Innocent then sided with John against the barons and in 1215 annulled Magna Carta. He also pressed Philip II of France to take back his wife Ingeborg of Denmark.

sections.h2: The Fourth Crusade and the Albigensian Crusade
paras: Innocent proclaimed the Fourth Crusade in 1198. Indebted to Venice, the crusaders attacked the Christian city of Zara in 1202, and Innocent excommunicated them. In 1204 they sacked Constantinople. Innocent condemned the atrocities, though he accepted the Latin Empire that resulted, and the sack deepened the division between Latin and Greek Christians.

After the murder of his legate Peter of Castelnau in 1208, Innocent called a crusade against the Cathars of southern France. The Albigensian Crusade became a long and brutal war in which northern French lords seized southern lands, an outcome far from the conversion Innocent had hoped for.

sections.h2: Francis, Dominic and the Fourth Lateran Council
paras: Around 1209 or 1210 Innocent gave oral approval to the simple rule of life presented by St. Francis of Assisi and his first companions, and he also encouraged St. Dominic's preaching mission. In November 1215 he opened the Fourth Lateran Council, counted as the twelfth ecumenical council and attended by hundreds of bishops and abbots.

Its seventy-one canons opened with a profession of faith that used the term transubstantiation for the Eucharist. Canon 21 required every Catholic who has reached the age of discretion to confess at least once a year and receive Communion at least at Easter, a precept still in force. Other canons forbade clergy to take part in trials by ordeal, restricted the founding of new religious rules, regulated preaching and clerical education, and required Jews and Muslims to wear distinctive dress. Innocent died at Perugia on July 16, 1216, while preparing a new crusade.

Reigned January 8, 1198 – July 16, 1216
Placed England under interdict (1208) and annulled Magna Carta (1215)
Called the Fourth Crusade, which sacked Constantinople in 1204
Approved St. Francis's way of life around 1209–1210
Convened the Fourth Lateran Council (1215)

faqs.question: What did the Fourth Lateran Council teach?
faqs.answer: It professed the Catholic faith using the term transubstantiation, required annual confession and Easter Communion, reformed clerical life, forbade clergy to take part in ordeals and restricted new religious rules, among its seventy-one canons.

faqs.question: Did Innocent III approve the sack of Constantinople?
faqs.answer: No. He had excommunicated the crusaders for attacking Zara and condemned the violence of 1204, though he later accepted the Latin Empire established there.

faqs.question: Why did Innocent III annul Magna Carta?
faqs.answer: King John had made England a papal fief in 1213, and Innocent viewed the charter as extorted from his vassal by force, so he declared it void in 1215.

directAnswer: Pope Honorius III was Cencio, a Roman cleric and longtime papal treasurer, who reigned from 1216 to 1227. He approved the Dominican Order, the final Rule of St. Francis and the Carmelite rule, launched the Fifth Crusade, and crowned Frederick II emperor.

sections.h2: Cencio, Camerarius and Author of the Liber Censuum
paras: Cencio was born in Rome; his traditional identification with the Savelli family is doubted by many historians. He was a canon of Santa Maria Maggiore and served as camerarius, the official in charge of papal finances. In 1192 he compiled the Liber Censuum, a register of the revenues owed to the Roman Church that remains a key source for medieval history.

Celestine III made him a cardinal, and he is often said to have been a tutor to the young Frederick II. He was elected at Perugia on July 18, 1216, two days after the death of Innocent III, when he was already elderly.

sections.h2: The Dominicans, Franciscans and Carmelites
paras: Honorius gave formal approval to several religious families that shaped the Church for centuries. On December 22, 1216, he confirmed the Order of Preachers founded by St. Dominic. On November 29, 1223, his bull Solet annuere approved the definitive Rule of the Friars Minor written by St. Francis, the text Franciscans still follow.

In 1226 he approved the rule given to the hermits of Mount Carmel by St. Albert of Jerusalem, a step in the recognition of the Carmelites. He also supported the Third Order movements that offered lay men and women a structured penitential life.

sections.h2: The Fifth Crusade and Frederick II
paras: Honorius made the recovery of Jerusalem the central goal of his reign. The Fifth Crusade sailed from 1217 and captured the Egyptian port of Damietta in 1219, but the crusaders refused an offer to exchange it for Jerusalem, marched on Cairo, and were forced to surrender in 1221.

Frederick II had taken the cross in 1215, and Honorius crowned him emperor in Rome on November 22, 1220, in expectation that he would lead the crusade. Frederick repeatedly delayed, and in 1225 at San Germano he agreed to set out by 1227 under pain of excommunication. Honorius did not live to see the outcome.

sections.h2: Canon Law and Final Years
paras: Honorius issued the Compilatio quinta, a collection of decretals sent to the University of Bologna in 1226, one of the first official papal law books. He was known for patience and mildness, preferring negotiation to confrontation. He died in Rome on March 18, 1227, and was buried in Santa Maria Maggiore.

faqs.question: Which religious orders did Honorius III approve?
faqs.answer: He confirmed the Dominicans in 1216, approved the final Rule of St. Francis with the bull Solet annuere in 1223, and approved the Carmelite rule in 1226.

faqs.question: What was the Liber Censuum?
faqs.answer: A register of payments owed to the Roman Church, compiled by Cencio in 1192 while he was papal treasurer. Historians still rely on it.

faqs.question: How did the Fifth Crusade turn out?
faqs.answer: Crusaders captured Damietta in Egypt in 1219, but after a failed advance on Cairo they surrendered the city in 1221 without regaining Jerusalem.

directAnswer: Pope Gregory IX was Ugolino of Segni, a kinsman of Innocent III and cardinal protector of the Franciscans, who reigned from 1227 to 1241. A friend of St. Francis and St. Clare, he canonized Francis, Anthony of Padua and Dominic, promulgated the Decretals that governed canon law for centuries, commissioned papal inquisitors, and fought a long struggle with Emperor Frederick II.

sections.h2: Ugolino, Friend of Francis and Clare
paras: Ugolino was born at Anagni into the family of the counts of Segni, the same family as Innocent III, who made him a cardinal in 1198. He became cardinal bishop of Ostia in 1206 and served as legate in Germany and northern Italy.

He knew St. Francis personally, and at Francis's request Honorius III named him protector of the Friars Minor. He also guided St. Clare and the Poor Ladies of San Damiano. He was elected pope on March 19, 1227, the day after Honorius died.

sections.h2: Canonizations and the Franciscan Movement
paras: Within two years of Francis's death, Gregory canonized him at Assisi on July 16, 1228, and laid the foundation stone of the basilica built in his honor. He canonized St. Anthony of Padua in 1232, less than a year after Anthony's death, St. Dominic in 1234, and St. Elizabeth of Hungary in 1235.

In 1230 his bull Quo elongati ruled that Francis's Testament was not legally binding on the friars and clarified how the brothers could use goods without owning them, decisions that shaped later Franciscan debates over poverty.

sections.h2: Frederick II and the Crusade
paras: When Frederick II again postponed his crusade in 1227, Gregory excommunicated him. Frederick sailed anyway in 1228 and in 1229 recovered Jerusalem by treaty with the sultan of Egypt. Pope and emperor reconciled at San Germano and Ceprano in 1230, but conflict over Lombardy and the Papal States led Gregory to excommunicate Frederick again in 1239.

In 1241 Frederick's fleet captured many prelates traveling to a council Gregory had summoned. With imperial troops near Rome, Gregory died on August 22, 1241. He also supported crusading campaigns in the Baltic region.

sections.h2: The Decretals, Paris and the Inquisition
paras: Gregory commissioned the Dominican St. Raymond of Peñafort to compile a single, official collection of papal decretals. Promulgated in 1234, the Decretals of Gregory IX, also called the Liber Extra, remained a core part of the Church's law until the Code of Canon Law of 1917. In 1231 his bull Parens scientiarum settled a strike at the University of Paris and confirmed the university's rights.

From the early 1230s Gregory commissioned inquisitors, chiefly Dominican friars, to investigate heresy under direct papal authority, which is regarded as the beginning of the papal inquisition. He also ordered an investigation of the Talmud in 1239, which led to its condemnation and burning in Paris in the 1240s, an episode now remembered as a grave injustice to the Jewish people.

faqs.question: How did Gregory IX know St. Francis?
faqs.answer: As Cardinal Ugolino he was the official protector of the Franciscan order and a personal friend of Francis, whom he canonized in 1228, less than two years after his death.

faqs.question: What were the Decretals of Gregory IX?
faqs.answer: An official collection of papal laws compiled by St. Raymond of Peñafort and promulgated in 1234. It remained central to Catholic canon law until 1917.

faqs.question: Did Gregory IX start the inquisition?
faqs.answer: He began appointing papal inquisitors, mostly Dominicans, in the early 1230s, which historians treat as the start of the papal inquisition, building on earlier bishops' inquiries.

directAnswer: Pope Celestine IV was Goffredo da Castiglione of Milan, cardinal bishop of Sabina, who was elected in October 1241 after a harsh confinement of the cardinals in Rome and died about two weeks later, before he could be crowned.

sections.h2: The Septizodium Election of 1241
paras: Goffredo came from Milan and served as a cardinal under Gregory IX, eventually as cardinal bishop of Sabina. When Gregory died in August 1241, Emperor Frederick II's forces were near Rome and two cardinals were his prisoners. The Roman senator Matteo Rosso Orsini locked the remaining cardinals in the ruined Septizodium on the Palatine to force a quick decision.

Conditions were severe in the summer heat, and the English cardinal Robert of Somercotes died during the confinement. This forced seclusion is often described as the first conclave in the strict sense. After weeks of deadlock the cardinals chose Goffredo on October 25, 1241.

sections.h2: Seventeen Days and a Long Vacancy
paras: Already elderly and apparently weakened by the ordeal, Celestine died on November 10, 1241, before his coronation. Almost no acts of his pontificate are recorded. Fearing a repeat of their confinement, many cardinals left Rome, and the Holy See remained vacant for about a year and a half, until the election of Innocent IV in June 1243. Little else is known about Celestine IV.

keyFacts: Personal name: Goffredo da Castiglione, of Milan
Reigned October 25 – November 10, 1241
Cardinal bishop of Sabina

Died before his coronation; followed by a vacancy of about nineteen months

faqs.question: Why was Celestine IV's election so difficult?
faqs.answer: Frederick II held two cardinals captive, and the rest were confined by Roman authorities in the Septizodium under harsh conditions until they agreed, a process in which one cardinal died.

faqs.question: Was Celestine IV ever crowned?
faqs.answer: No. He died on November 10, 1241, about seventeen days after his election, before a coronation could take place.

directAnswer: Pope Innocent IV was Sinibaldo Fieschi of Genoa, a leading canon lawyer who reigned from 1243 to 1254. He fled to Lyon, where the First Council of Lyon in 1245 declared Emperor Frederick II deposed, sent friars as envoys to the Mongols, approved the Rule of St. Clare, and issued the bull Ad extirpanda permitting torture in heresy trials.

sections.h2: Sinibaldo Fieschi, Canonist of Bologna
paras: Sinibaldo belonged to the Fieschi family, counts of Lavagna in the Republic of Genoa. He studied and taught law at Bologna and wrote a commentary on the Decretals of Gregory IX that made him one of the most influential canonists of the Middle Ages; later jurists often credited him with the idea of a corporation as a legal person. Gregory IX made him a cardinal and vice-chancellor of the Roman Church.
After the long vacancy that followed Celestine IV's death, he was elected at Anagni on June 25, 1243.

sections.h2: Flight to Lyon and the Deposition of Frederick II
paras: Negotiations with Frederick II failed, and in 1244 Innocent escaped secretly to Genoa and then to Lyon, beyond the emperor's reach. There he convened the First Council of Lyon, counted as the thirteenth ecumenical council. On July 17, 1245, the council declared Frederick deposed and his subjects freed from their allegiance. The council also addressed the Mongol threat and support for the Latin East. Tradition holds that the red hat was first given to cardinals at this time.

The struggle continued after Frederick's death in 1250 against his sons Conrad IV and Manfred. Innocent returned to Italy in 1251 and spent his last years trying to secure the Kingdom of Sicily for a ruler loyal to the Holy See.

sections.h2: Envoys to the Mongols and New Saints
paras: In 1245 Innocent sent the Franciscan John of Plano Carpini on a long journey to the court of the Mongol Great Khan, carrying letters urging peace and the Christian faith. Other missions, including Dominicans, were sent by different routes. Carpini's account of his journey became one of the earliest European descriptions of the Mongols.

Innocent canonized St. Peter of Verona in 1253, less than a year after his martyrdom, and St. Stanislaus of Kraków the same year. On August 9, 1253, he approved the Rule written by St. Clare of Assisi, the first rule for women religious written by a woman, two days before her death.

sections.h2: Ad extirpanda and Its Legacy
paras: In May 1252 Innocent issued the bull Ad extirpanda, which directed civil authorities in Italian cities to set up machinery for prosecuting heresy and allowed them to use torture to obtain confessions, provided it did not cause loss of limb or death. The decree marked a dark turn in the history of the inquisition, and the Church has since acknowledged the wrongs committed in the name of faith during such proceedings.
Innocent IV died at Naples on December 7, 1254.

keyFacts: Personal name: Sinibaldo Fieschi, of Genoa
Reigned June 25, 1243 – December 7, 1254
Leading canon lawyer, author of a commentary on the Decretals
Convened the First Council of Lyon (1245), which declared Frederick II deposed
Approved the Rule of St. Clare (August 9, 1253)
Issued Ad extirpanda (1252) permitting torture in heresy cases

faqs.question: Why did Innocent IV hold a council at Lyon?
faqs.answer: Frederick II's power in Italy made Rome unsafe, so Innocent fled to Lyon in 1244. The council there in 1245 declared the emperor deposed.

faqs.question: What did the bull Ad extirpanda allow?
faqs.answer: Issued in 1252, it permitted civil authorities prosecuting heresy to use torture to obtain confessions, within limits that forbade causing death or loss of limb.

faqs.question: What was Innocent IV's connection to St. Clare?
faqs.answer: He visited Clare in her final illness and approved her Rule on August 9, 1253, two days before she died.
